title: Corpus Christi Started Pumping Groundwater at “Lightning Speed.” Rural Residents Fear the Consequences.
author: Rachel Denny Clow
content:
Late in 2024, Corpus Christi, Texas, was desperate for water after years of
drought. So city officials hatched a plan to tap millions of gallons of water
a day from an aquifer that serves dozens of counties across the Texas Gulf
Coast.

The city would drill wells — lots of them.

Corpus Christi’s drilling frenzy alarmed rural residents, who worried it
threatened their access to water. They [mobilized to create a groundwater
conservation district](https://www.kristv.com/news/local-news/in-your-
neighborhood/corpus-christi/residents-push-for-first-groundwater-district-in-
nueces-county) that would regulate drilling and, they hoped, limit how much
water the city could pump.

Then Corpus Christi officials came up with a peculiar idea. Fearing the
residents’ effort could hamper the city’s ambitious plans to tap significant
amounts of groundwater, officials asked a local entity to serve as its well
regulator.

The advantages: City Council members appoint that entity’s board of directors,
and its staff is made up entirely of city employees.

Since that decision last fall, the entity — called the Corpus Christi Aquifer
Storage and Recovery Conservation District — has greenlit every city request
to drill more wells. In doing so, The Texas Tribune and KRIS 6 found, it fast-
tracked its permitting process for the city and overlooked steps that would
have slowed down the process for approving the permits — safeguards its own
rules require to protect other well users.

A city-commissioned study released this summer found that the drilling plan
could cause land around the wells to sink and water levels in other nearby
wells to drop significantly. But by then, the district had already approved
permits allowing the city to pump up to about 40 million gallons a day from 20
wells, although the city draws less than a third of that daily on average.

The city defended the approvals. It said the district’s rules let the board
decide when it has enough information to sign off on a permit and that before
it does so, the city gives estimates of how pumping could affect water levels.

But water experts warn that the amount the city is allowed to pump in such a
small area is exorbitant. “It’s absolutely unfathomable,” said Drew Molly, the
former chief operating officer of Corpus Christi’s water department.  

Molly, who is now chief water officer at Houston’s water department, said the
district’s “lightning speed” approval of the city’s permits will cause ripple
effects locally and across the state.

In Texas, fights over limited groundwater supplies will likely intensify as
the population booms. Groundwater comes from aquifers and [makes up more than
half of the state’s water
supply](https://www.texastribune.org/2025/05/29/texas-water-crisis-
groundwater-rights/).

Aquifers stretch underground across counties and, sometimes, across states.
The aquifer Corpus Christi draws from serves dozens of communities along the
Gulf of Mexico, including some in Louisiana. Overpumping from aquifers is a
key concern in Texas because they need rain and time to refill. As droughts
get longer, the state’s water plan shows [larger drops in groundwater’s
availability](https://www.propublica.org/article/water-aquifers-groundwater-
rising-ocean-levels) compared with other sources.

Groundwater pumping must be approached with caution, experts say. In worst-
case scenarios, excessive pumping “can wipe an aquifer out,” said Jarrod
Reynolds, a groundwater resource engineer.

“It can be a stopgap, it can be a supplement, but it’s something that’s got to
be managed,” Reynolds said.

Corpus Christi’s rapid expansion of groundwater wells offers a critical, if
not extreme, example of the challenges presented by a patchwork system for
regulating the water that cities, businesses and citizens can extract from the
ground.

The coastal city of more than 300,000 residents nearly reached a crisis point
earlier this year after persistent drought and years of inaction. It was
months away from being unable to meet water demand and faced harsh
restrictions to conserve supplies.

Drilling for groundwater became an important fix. So when the possibility of
tougher regulation loomed in the wake of the rural residents’ efforts, city
officials turned to Corpus Christi’s storage and recovery district, an entity
created two decades earlier with the power to approve well permits.

The storage and recovery district is one of nearly 100 such groundwater
districts in the state, but it’s the only one with City Council-appointed
leaders. Most groundwater districts are led by leaders who are either elected
or appointed by county officials — an important distinction since counties are
not water suppliers, so there is less concern about any conflict of interest.

Corpus Christi leaders insisted in a written statement that the close ties the
city shares with its well regulator will not hamstring efforts to protect the
aquifer.

“There is no conflict of interest. City employees involved with the District
have no personal or financial interest in permitting decisions,” said Ashley
Marion, strategic business manager for the city water department, in the
written statement. She added that, “The City and District share an interest in
protecting and sustainably managing regional groundwater.”

Marion also said the city tracks water levels and physical conditions at the
wells and adjusts pumping rates based on daily data and long-term modeling.

But the arrangement has drawn concern from water experts across the state, an
outgoing state lawmaker and at least one of the storage and recovery
district’s own board members.

“That’s the fox guarding the henhouse,” said Robert Mace, executive director
at Texas State University’s Meadows Center for Water and the Environment,
which focuses on water and environmental management policy.

“It tells me that the district is looking out for Corpus Christi’s interests
and not necessarily the interests of other landowners that might be affected.”

### Years of Inaction Lead to a City in Crisis

Corpus Christi’s decision to begin drilling wells reflects how the city’s
approach to finding water swings wildly during drought.

The city currently relies on three drought-vulnerable reservoirs for most of
its supply. Despite warnings that it needed to diversify its water sources,
the city has repeatedly waffled on whether to invest in long-term solutions.

Since 2025, a divided City Council has twice declined to move forward with a
city-run desalination plant, even though the state had approved [$757 million
in loans](https://www.texastribune.org/2026/03/17/texas-corpus-christi-water-
supply-guide-city-council-meeting/) [for the
project](https://www.kristv.com/news/local-news/in-your-neighborhood/corpus-
christi/abbott-says-corpus-christi-squandered-750-million-in-state-water-
funds-heres-what-the-money-actually-is) and Corpus Christi officials had
selected contractors to begin the work. The city has said the plant could
produce around a third of the city’s daily demand.

After the most recent vote in September, outgoing [Gov. Greg Abbott
chastised](https://www.kristv.com/news/local-news/in-your-neighborhood/corpus-
christi/inner-harbor-desalination-project-stalls-again-after-city-council-
vote) Corpus Christi leaders for having “once again failed to secure reliable
water.”

Desalination was not the city’s only missed opportunity to increase its water
supply. Two decades ago, Democratic state Sen. Juan “Chuy” Hinojosa authored
legislation that created the Corpus Christi Aquifer Storage and Recovery
Conservation District. The district’s purpose is in its name: The city had
plans to inject and store excess drinking water and treated wastewater
underground to save for emergencies. Hinojosa did not respond to a request for
comment for this story.

In the years that followed, the district studied the idea, drilled test wells
and drew up plans. But nothing ever happened.  

As the region’s main reservoirs were drying up in late 2024, city leaders
found themselves searching for solutions again. Molly, then the city’s water
director, had a “wild idea.” He reached out to John Michael, an engineer long
involved in the city’s water projects, to ask if the city could drill wells
along the Nueces River, according to a recent memo in which Michael recalled
the conversation.

It was possible, and [the city quickly started
drilling](https://www.texastribune.org/2026/01/12/texas-corpus-christi-water-
crisis-desalination-plant-wells/). But this was always supposed to be a
temporary solution.

While the wells were “a viable option to supplement water resources during the
current drought, I never envisioned that the wells would be used for anything
other than emergency supply,” Michael wrote in the June 26 memo.

In a written response to the newsrooms, the city called the groundwater
program “a key component” of its strategy to diversify the region’s water
supply.

Then officials learned of rural residents’ efforts to form their own
groundwater conservation district. This posed a “potential danger” to the
city’s plans, said then-Corpus Christi City Attorney Miles Risley at an
October 2025 City Council meeting.

So the city moved quickly to ask the storage and recovery district to expand
its boundaries to include its well fields outside city limits in Nueces
County.

“Do you think we’d be able to carry that out without being biased?” council
member Everett Roy asked the city’s water resource manager, Esteban Ramos, as
the council debated asking the entity to regulate the wells.

“Yes, I do,” answered Ramos, who is also the storage and recovery district’s
general manager.

When the storage and recovery district approved the city’s well permits last
year,**** board members attached several protective requirements, such as
creating plans to monitor water quality in its well fields and to reduce harm
to neighbors’ wells.

None of those requirements prevented or slowed the city from moving forward
with its drilling plans.

The city has not “fully satisfied” some of those requirements nine months
later, according to a document two board members prepared for the district.
The city said the district asked it to provide more information on its
monitoring and mitigation plan. It said it is working with the district to
meet the conditions and that the city’s compliance reports are public.

A private research company named Intera raised several red flags about the
city’s groundwater pumping in a study the city released in June. It estimated
that the ground around the city’s western well fields could sink about 20
inches over the next 30 years.

As water is withdrawn, just a few inches of sinkage can do costly damage to
infrastructure, including pipelines, foundations, roads and bridges.

This type of sinkage, caused by compacting sand, rock or sediment, can reduce
the amount of water an aquifer can hold long term, according to the American
Geosciences Institute.

A drop in the aquifer’s levels would first be felt by rural residents, whose
wells are not as deep as the city’s. The study said a drop of up to 100 feet
was possible within five years near the city’s wells. In its response to these
findings, the city maintained that they are just projections and don’t reflect
how much it’s pumping on average.

But the city can easily pump more in emergencies, like when pipes break or
during long dry spells.  

That’s the fear of rural residents like Scott Barraza, who lives on 20 acres
about 20 miles from downtown Corpus Christi with his wife, Julie; teen
daughter, Grace; five dogs; three goats; and a horse named Rosie.

He recently purchased a $9,000 water purification system and a trailer to haul
water from the city for his family and neighbors. Barraza acknowledges it’s
probably excessive but says it’s best to be prepared.

“When you live out in the country, you don’t have a city water supply. Your
well is your water supply,” he said.

Molly said the city’s decision to increasingly rely on groundwater rather than
investing in a seawater desalination plant means Corpus Christi “basically put
all their eggs in a terrible basket.”

### Who Guards Groundwater?

What’s happening in Corpus Christi and the surrounding area raises critical
questions about how the state manages its limited groundwater resources and
who regulates them.

Republican state Rep. [Denise
Villalobos](https://directory.texastribune.org/denise-villalobos/) was so
concerned about the unusual dynamic in Corpus Christi that she planned to file
a bill to abolish the storage and recovery district in the upcoming
legislative session. She also drafted another bill to create, in its place, a
more traditional groundwater district that would regulate wells across all of
Nueces County.

Then she lost her seat to [Democrat Stephanie Guerrero
Sáenz](https://www.kristv.com/news/political/elections/villalobos-concedes-
texas-house-district-34-race-to-stephanie-guerrero-saenz) in the recent
midterm elections. The incoming lawmaker, whose term begins in January, was
less certain about her approach when interviewed by the newsrooms, saying she
needs to talk with her new constituents first. She said any legislation she
supports “must strike the right balance between protecting rural groundwater
rights and addressing the urgent water needs of our region.”

In the meantime, some members of the storage and recovery district are
starting to push back, including Michael, the engineer. He was appointed to
the board five weeks after the district approved the city’s first 20 well
permits.

Next month, the board is set to consider a resolution that would cap the
city’s pumping to 6.5 million gallons a day — half of the city’s current
average — until it meets the regulatory requirements meant to protect the
aquifer’s health.

Michael and board member Jeff Edmonds, who is also the city’s director of
engineering, proposed the measure, which is set for discussion Dec. 3. They
said the current rate of the city’s pumping could cause “irreversible offsite
impacts.” They also point to civil penalties the city risks if it continues to
not comply with the rules.

For now, the recent water crisis in Corpus Christi has been [averted after
rains this summer](https://www.texastribune.org/2026/07/27/corpus-christi-
water-texas-floodwater-emergency/) temporarily refilled the reservoirs the
city depends on. But projections show the city could be back in a water
emergency by [September 2029](https://www.texastribune.org/2026/07/24/texas-
corpus-christi-flood-water-gains-lakes-choke-canyon/).

It’s a reminder of the reality that faces the entire state. The Texas Water
Development Board has said Texas [does not have enough water to meet
demand](https://www.texastribune.org/2025/03/13/texas-water-explained-supply-
demand/) if it faces a historic drought.

What’s happening with the storage and recovery district is “a microcosm of
examples of what’s happening around the state,” Michael told the newsrooms,
because Texas’ population is growing as available water resources are
dwindling.

“We have to manage these districts in a sustainable manner,” he said, “and
decisions have to be made on science and not emotions.”
